rules.statement: A builder type that lets callers register services (such as an endpoint-group builder) should inherit `IServiceBuilder` from `NCode.Registration`, not expose a bare `IServiceCollection`, so you don't end up with a second registration surface running alongside it.
rules.why: A bare `IServiceCollection` can't reach builder-level helpers such as `AddMessageFactory<T>()`, and it splits registration into two parallel vocabularies.
rules.check: Look for new or changed builder/context interfaces that expose an `IServiceCollection Services` property for registration where they could inherit `IServiceBuilder`.

rules.statement: Register each endpoint family through one extension on the endpoint-group builder. That extension registers the family's endpoint provider and the services it depends on, and nothing else registers the same endpoints a second time.
rules.why: Keeping the registration next to the endpoint gives one place to register everything. A separate per-family registration chain made the same endpoints appear twice.
rules.check: Look for endpoints or endpoint providers registered in more than one place, or for an endpoint's dependent services (including message factories) registered in a separate chain instead of with the endpoint group.

rules.statement: Put generic, domain-agnostic infrastructure (routing plumbing, generic operation/result types) in a cross-cutting package whose namespace matches its purpose, not in a domain-specific package or namespace.
rules.why: Generic plumbing tied to a domain package can't be reused, and the domain namespace misdescribes what it does.
rules.check: Look for new types in a domain package (for example `*.Identity.*`) that contain no domain-specific logic, or generic types given domain-specific names such as `MapIdentityEndpoints`.

rules.statement: Keep core DI/registration packages free of ASP.NET Core dependencies. Put ASP.NET Core-specific extensions in a separate `*.AspNetCore` package that depends on the core package.
rules.why: Keeping the core package pure DI means any consumer can adopt it, and only consumers that need the ASP.NET Core concern take on that dependency.
rules.check: Look for `FrameworkReference Microsoft.AspNetCore.App`, ASP.NET Core package references, or `Microsoft.AspNetCore.*` usings added to a core registration or abstractions package that has no `.AspNetCore` suffix.
